title: Parametric vs non-parametric tests, and the key non-parametric tests
summary: The side-by-side comparison of parametric and non-parametric tests, why and when to use non-parametric tests, and the four key non-parametric tests with their business applications.

chunks.heading: Parametric vs non-parametric: the comparison table
chunks.explanation_md:
Learn this table row by row:

| Basis | Parametric tests | Non-parametric tests |
|---|---|---|
| Data type | Interval or ratio (continuous) | Ordinal or nominal |
| Distribution | Assumes normality | No assumption of distribution |
| Measure | Mean and SD | Medians and ranks |
| Example tests | t-test, ANOVA, regression | Chi-square, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis |
| Sample size | Usually large | Works with small samples |
| Use when | Data is symmetric, continuous | Data is skewed or categorical |
chunks.exam_line: Parametric: interval/ratio data, assumes normality, uses mean and SD, large samples (t-test, ANOVA, regression). Non-parametric: ordinal/nominal, no distribution assumption, medians and ranks, small samples (chi-square, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis).

chunks.heading: Four key non-parametric tests
chunks.explanation_md:
| Test | Type | Used when | Business application |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chi-square** | Categorical | Compare **observed vs expected frequencies** | Market share, preference counts |
| **Wilcoxon Signed-Rank** | Dependent (paired) | Compare **medians of matched data** | Pre/post customer feedback |
| **Mann-Whitney U** | Independent | Test differences between **two independent groups** | Compare supplier ratings |
| **Kruskal-Wallis** | Multiple groups | Compare **3+ independent groups** | Customer satisfaction across regions |

A useful way to hold these in your head: Wilcoxon is the paired case, Mann-Whitney U is the two-independent-groups case, and Kruskal-Wallis is the three-or-more-groups case.
chunks.exam_line: Chi-square: observed vs expected frequencies; Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: paired medians; Mann-Whitney U: two independent groups; Kruskal-Wallis: 3+ independent groups.

questions.stem: Why are non-parametric tests used? Give the reasons listed in the module.
questions.model_answer_md:
Non-parametric tests are the fallback when parametric conditions do not hold.

- The **data does not meet parametric assumptions** (normality, homogeneity).
- The **data is ordinal or categorical**, such as ranked preferences or satisfaction ratings.
- **Small samples or outliers distort means.**
- They are **useful in Six Sigma, quality control, customer satisfaction or survey data** environments.

The slide on parametric tests makes the same point: when assumptions are violated, non-parametric tests are recommended.

questions.stem: A company collects pre and post customer feedback ratings from the same customers after a service change. The ratings are ordinal. Which test should it use and why?
questions.model_answer_md:
The data and design point to one test.

- **Design:** the same customers are rated **before and after**, so the data are **dependent (paired), matched data**.
- **Data type:** the ratings are **ordinal**, which is a reason to use a **non-parametric** test.
- **Test:** the **Wilcoxon Signed-Rank** test, which **compares medians of matched data**; the slide's application is exactly **pre/post customer feedback**.

So Wilcoxon Signed-Rank is the right choice.

Ordinal data calls for non-parametric
Wilcoxon Signed-Rank, compares medians of matched data

questions.stem: Differentiate between parametric and non-parametric tests, and explain when a researcher should switch to a non-parametric test.
questions.model_answer_md:
Statistical tests fall into two families, and the data decide which to use.

| Basis | Parametric tests | Non-parametric tests |
|---|---|---|
| **Data type** | Interval or ratio (continuous) | Ordinal or nominal |
| **Distribution** | Assumes normality | No assumption of distribution |
| **Measure** | Mean and SD | Medians and ranks |
| **Example tests** | t-test, ANOVA, regression | Chi-square, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis |
| **Sample size** | Usually large | Works with small samples |
| **Use when** | Data is symmetric, continuous | Data is skewed or categorical |

**Strength of parametric tests:** they are **powerful and efficient** when their assumptions are met, giving **precise estimates**. Their assumptions are quantitative data, a normal population, homogeneity of variance and independence of observations.

**When to switch to a non-parametric test:**
- the **data does not meet parametric assumptions** (normality, homogeneity);
- the **data is ordinal or categorical**, such as ranked preferences or satisfaction ratings;
- **small samples or outliers distort the means**.

The parametric slide gives the same warning: **violating assumptions can lead to misleading results**, and **non-parametric tests are then recommended**. They are especially useful in **Six Sigma, quality control, customer satisfaction and survey data**.

**Conclusion:** parametric tests are more precise when their assumptions hold; non-parametric tests are safer when the data are ranked, categorical, skewed or few.

questions.stem: For each business situation, choose the right non-parametric test and justify it: (a) checking whether preference counts for brands match expected frequencies; (b) comparing supplier ratings between two independent groups; (c) comparing customer satisfaction across four regions; (d) comparing pre and post customer feedback from the same customers.
questions.model_answer_md:
Each non-parametric test fits a different design, so we match the design to the test.

**(a) Preference counts vs expected frequencies: Chi-square.** The data are **categorical counts**, and chi-square **compares observed vs expected frequencies**. Its listed applications are **market share and preference counts**.

**(b) Supplier ratings, two independent groups: Mann-Whitney U.** The two groups are **independent**, and Mann-Whitney U **tests differences between two independent groups**; comparing supplier ratings is its listed application.

**(c) Satisfaction across four regions: Kruskal-Wallis.** Four regions means **3+ independent groups**, which Kruskal-Wallis compares; **customer satisfaction across regions** is its listed application.

**(d) Pre and post feedback from the same customers: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank.** The data are **dependent (paired)**, and Wilcoxon **compares medians of matched data**, with **pre/post customer feedback** as its application.

**Why non-parametric at all:** ratings and preferences are **ordinal or categorical**, and these tests work with **medians and ranks** and make **no distribution assumption**, which suits customer satisfaction and survey data.

**Conclusion:** frequencies go to chi-square, two groups to Mann-Whitney U, three or more groups to Kruskal-Wallis, and matched pairs to Wilcoxon.

rubric.point: (a) Chi-square: observed vs expected frequencies
(b) Mann-Whitney U: two independent groups
(c) Kruskal-Wallis: 3+ independent groups
(d) Wilcoxon Signed-Rank: matched data
Ordinal or categorical data, medians and ranks, no distribution assumption
